title: Part 1, Chapter 29
paragraphs: Which describes the comical trick and strategy used to rescue our lovesick knight from the harsh penance he had imposed on himself

“That, gentlemen, is the true story of my sad misfortunes. Judge for yourselves now whether the sighs and laments you heard, and the tears that ran from my eyes, didn’t have cause enough — even if I had given way to them far more freely. And once you consider the nature of my disaster, you will see that consolation is pointless, because there is no possible cure for it. All I ask of you — and it is something you can do easily and reasonably — is to show me a place where I can spend my life without being hounded by the fear and dread of being found by the people searching for me. I know the great love my parents have for me would guarantee me a kind welcome from them, but the shame I feel at the mere thought that I cannot stand before them as the person they expect is so overwhelming that I would rather banish myself from their sight forever than look them in the face knowing they were seeing mine stripped of the purity they had every right to expect from me.”

With those words she fell silent, and the color flooding her face showed plainly the pain and shame she was suffering inside. The listeners felt as much pity as amazement at her misfortunes, and the curate was just about to offer her some comfort and advice when Cardenio got there first. “So then, señora,” he said, “you are the beautiful Dorothea, the only daughter of the wealthy Clenardo?” Dorothea was astonished to hear her father’s name, and astonished at the miserable appearance of the man who spoke it — it has already been described how wretchedly Cardenio was dressed. So she said to him:
“And who might you be, brother, that you seem to know my father’s name so well? Because as far as I can remember, I haven’t mentioned it once in the whole story of my misfortunes.”

“I am that unhappy man, señora,” Cardenio replied, “the one who, as you said, Luscinda declared to be her husband. I am the unfortunate Cardenio, and the wrongdoing of the same man who brought you to your present condition has reduced me to the state you see: bare, ragged, deprived of all human comfort and — worse still — of my reason, since I only have it during the brief stretches when Heaven chooses to give it back to me. I, Dorothea, am the man who witnessed the wrong Don Fernando committed, who stood there waiting to hear the ‘Yes’ by which Luscinda declared herself his betrothed. I am the man who didn’t have the courage to see how her fainting fit ended, or what came of the paper found in her bodice, because my heart didn’t have the strength to endure so many blows of bad fortune at once. So I lost all patience and left the house, and after leaving a letter with my host, begging him to put it into Luscinda’s hands, I made my way to these wild solitudes, determined to end here a life I hated as though it were my mortal enemy. But fate refused to take that life from me, and settled for taking my reason instead — perhaps to preserve me for the good luck I have just had in meeting you. Because if what you have told us is true, and I believe it is, it may be that Heaven still has a happier ending in store for both our misfortunes than we expect. Since Luscinda cannot marry Don Fernando — she is mine, as she herself declared so openly — and Don Fernando cannot marry her because he is yours, we can reasonably hope that Heaven will give back to each of us what belongs to us, since it still exists and has not yet been signed away or destroyed. And since we have this consolation, born of no far-fetched hope or wild fantasy, I beg you, señora, to make new resolutions in your better judgment, as I intend to make in mine, and to prepare yourself to look forward to better fortune. I swear to you, on my faith as a gentleman and a Christian, not to desert you until I see you in possession of Don Fernando. And if I cannot persuade him with words to acknowledge what he owes you, I will then use the right my rank as a gentleman gives me and challenge him with just cause for the injury he has done you — setting aside my own wrongs, which I will leave to Heaven to avenge, while here on earth I devote myself to yours.”

Cardenio’s words completed Dorothea’s astonishment. Not knowing how to give thanks for such an offer, she tried to kiss his feet, but Cardenio wouldn’t allow it, and the licentiate answered for them both. He praised Cardenio’s sound reasoning, and then begged, advised, and urged them to come with him to his village, where they could supply themselves with whatever they needed and work out how to find Don Fernando, or return Dorothea to her parents, or do whatever seemed best to them. Cardenio and Dorothea thanked him and accepted his kind offer. The barber, who had been listening to everything attentively and in silence, added some kind words of his own, and with as much goodwill as the curate he offered his services in any way that might be useful to them. He also explained to them briefly the purpose that had brought the two of them there, along with the strange nature of Don Quixote’s madness, and that they were waiting for his squire, who had gone off to look for him. Like the memory of a dream, the quarrel he had had with Don Quixote came back to Cardenio, and he described it to the others — though he couldn’t say what the argument had been about.

At that moment they heard a shout and recognized it as Sancho Panza, who was calling out loudly because he hadn’t found them where he’d left them. They went to meet him, and when they asked about Don Quixote, he told them how he had found him stripped to his shirt, gaunt, yellow, half dead with hunger, and sighing for his lady Dulcinea. Sancho had told him that she ordered him to leave that place and come to El Toboso, where she was waiting for him, but he had answered that he was determined not to appear before her beauty until he had done deeds that made him worthy of her favor. If this kept up, Sancho said, his master ran the risk of never becoming an emperor, as he was duty-bound to do, or even an archbishop, which was the least he could be — so they really needed to think about how to get him away from there. The licentiate told him in reply not to worry: they would get him out of there whether he liked it or not. He then told Cardenio and Dorothea what they had planned for curing Don Quixote, or at least getting him home. At that, Dorothea said she could play the damsel in distress better than the barber could — especially since she had with her the very dress to do it convincingly — and that they could trust her to act the part exactly as the scheme required in every detail, because she had read a great many books of chivalry and knew precisely the style in which afflicted damsels begged favors from knights-errant.

“In that case,” said the curate, “there’s nothing left to do but get started right away. Fortune is clearly declaring itself in our favor, since it has so unexpectedly opened a door for your relief and smoothed the road toward our goal.”

Dorothea then pulled out of her pillowcase a full petticoat of some rich fabric and a green mantle of another fine material, along with a necklace and other jewelry from a little box, and in an instant she had dressed herself up so that she looked like a great and wealthy lady. All this, and more, she said, she had taken from home in case she needed it, though until now she’d had no occasion to use it. They were all delighted by her grace, her bearing, and her beauty, and they declared Don Fernando a man of very poor taste for rejecting such charms. But the one who admired her most was Sancho Panza, because it seemed to him — and it was true — that in all the days of his life he had never seen so lovely a creature. He eagerly asked the curate who this beautiful lady was and what she was doing in this out-of-the-way place.

“This fair lady, brother Sancho,” the curate replied, “is no less a person than the heiress in the direct male line of the great kingdom of Micomicon. She has come in search of your master to beg a favor of him — namely, that he right a wrong, an injury that a wicked giant has done her. And because of the fame as a good knight that your master has won far and wide, this princess has come all the way from Guinea to find him.”

“A lucky search and a lucky find!” said Sancho Panza at this. “Especially if my master has the good luck to right that injury and fix that wrong by killing that son of a bitch of a giant your worship mentions — and kill him he will if he meets him, unless the giant turns out to be a phantom, because my master has no power at all against phantoms. But there’s one thing among others I’d beg of you, señor licentiate: to stop my master from taking a fancy to becoming an archbishop, which is what I’m afraid of, your worship should advise him to marry this princess right away. That way he’ll be disqualified from taking archbishop’s orders, he’ll come into his empire easily, and I’ll get to the end of what I’ve been wanting. I’ve thought the matter over carefully, and as far as I can work out, it won’t do for me if my master becomes an archbishop, because I’m no use to the Church — I’m married. And for a man like me, with a wife and children, to start chasing dispensations so I could hold a paying position in the Church would be endless work. So, señor, it all comes down to my master marrying this lady right away — though I don’t yet know her grace, so I can’t call her by her name.”
“She is called Princess Micomicona,” said the curate, “for since her kingdom is Micomicon, it’s obvious that must be her name.”

“No doubt about that,” Sancho replied. “I’ve known plenty of people who take their name and title from the place they were born, calling themselves Pedro of Alcalá, Juan of Úbeda, or Diego of Valladolid. Maybe over there in Guinea the queens do the same thing and take the names of their kingdoms.”

“That may well be,” said the curate, “and as for your master’s marriage, I’ll do everything in my power to help it along.” Sancho was as pleased by this as the curate was amazed at his simplicity, and at seeing how thoroughly his master’s absurdities had taken hold of his imagination — for Sancho had clearly convinced himself that Don Quixote was going to become an emperor.

By now Dorothea had seated herself on the curate’s mule and the barber had fitted the ox-tail beard to his face, and they told Sancho to lead them to where Don Quixote was, warning him not to let on that he knew either the licentiate or the barber, since his master’s becoming an emperor depended entirely on his not recognizing them. Neither the curate nor Cardenio thought it wise to go along, though — Cardenio in case he reminded Don Quixote of the quarrel they had had, and the curate because his presence wasn’t needed just yet. So they let the others ride on ahead while they followed slowly on foot. The curate didn’t forget to coach Dorothea on how to act, but she told them not to worry: everything would be done exactly as the books of chivalry required and described.

They had gone about three-quarters of a league when they spotted Don Quixote in a wilderness of rocks, dressed by now, though not in his armor. The moment Dorothea saw him and was told by Sancho that this was Don Quixote, she whipped her palfrey forward, with the well-bearded barber following. When they reached him, her squire leapt down from his mule and came forward to lift her down in his arms, and she, dismounting with great ease of manner, went and knelt at Don Quixote’s feet. Although he tried to raise her up, she stayed kneeling and addressed him like this:

“I will not rise from this spot, brave and mighty knight, until your goodness and courtesy grant me a favor — one that will add to the honor and renown of your person, and serve the most desolate and afflicted damsel the sun has ever looked upon. And if the strength of your powerful arm matches the reputation of your immortal fame, then you are bound to help a helpless woman who, drawn by the scent of your famous name, has come from far-off lands to seek your aid in her misfortunes.”
“I will not answer a single word, beautiful lady,” Don Quixote replied, “nor will I hear anything more about your situation, until you rise from the ground.”
“I will not rise, señor,” answered the afflicted damsel, “unless, of your courtesy, the favor I ask is granted to me first.”
“I grant it and accord it,” said Don Quixote, “provided it can be carried out without damage or harm to my king, my country, or the lady who holds the key to my heart and my freedom.”

“It will bring no damage or harm to any of them, my good lord,” said the afflicted damsel — and at this point Sancho Panza sidled up close to his master’s ear and whispered very softly, “Your worship can grant the favor she’s asking with complete safety. It’s nothing at all — just killing one big giant — and the lady asking is the exalted Princess Micomicona, queen of the great kingdom of Micomicon in Ethiopia.”

“Let her be whoever she may,” Don Quixote replied. “I will do what my duty demands and what my conscience tells me, in keeping with the vows of my profession.” Then, turning to the damsel, he said, “Let your great beauty rise, for I grant the favor you would ask of me.”

“Then what I ask,” said the damsel, “is that your magnanimous person come with me at once, wherever I lead you, and that you promise not to take on any other adventure or quest until you have avenged me on a traitor who, against every human and divine law, has usurped my kingdom.”

“I repeat that I grant it,” Don Quixote replied. “And so, lady, from this day forward you can set aside the sadness that weighs on you and let your failing hopes take on new life and strength. With the help of God and of my arm, you will soon see yourself restored to your kingdom and seated on the throne of your ancient and mighty realm, in defiance of every villain who would deny it. And now, hands to the work — for in delay, they say, lies danger.”

The distressed damsel made a stubborn effort to kiss his hands, but Don Quixote, who was in all things a polished and courteous knight, would not allow it on any account. Instead he made her rise and embraced her with great courtesy and politeness, then ordered Sancho to check Rocinante’s girths and to arm him without a moment’s delay. Sancho took down the armor, which was hanging from a tree like a trophy, and after seeing to the girths he had his master armed in an instant. As soon as Don Quixote found himself in his armor, he exclaimed:
“Let us go, in God’s name, to bring help to this great lady.”

The barber was on his knees all this while, taking great pains to hide his laughter and keep his beard from falling off — because if it had fallen, their whole fine scheme might have collapsed. But now, seeing the favor granted and the speed with which Don Quixote was preparing to set out and fulfill it, he stood up and took his lady’s hand, and between the two of them they lifted her onto the mule. Don Quixote then mounted Rocinante, and the barber settled onto his own animal, leaving Sancho to travel on foot — which made him feel the loss of his Dapple all over again, missing him badly now. But he bore it all cheerfully, convinced that his master was now well and truly launched and on the very point of becoming an emperor; he had no doubt at all that Don Quixote would marry this princess and end up at least king of Micomicon. The only thing that troubled him was the thought that this kingdom was in the land of the blacks, and that the people they would give him as vassals would all be black. But his imagination soon found a remedy for that, and he said to himself, “What does it matter to me if my vassals are black? What do I have to do but load them up as cargo and carry them to Spain, where I can sell them and get paid in cash, and use the money to buy some title or some office and live at my ease for the rest of my days? Yes — unless you fall asleep and don’t have the wit or skill to turn things to your advantage and sell three, six, or ten thousand vassals while you’re still talking about it! By God, I’ll move them all, big and small, however I can, and however black they are, I’ll turn them into white or yellow coin. Come on, come on — what a fool I am!” And so he trudged along, so wrapped up in his thoughts and so easy in his mind that he forgot all about the hardship of traveling on foot.

Cardenio and the curate were watching all this from behind some bushes, unsure how to join the group. But the curate, who was quick with schemes, soon hit on a way to manage it: with a pair of scissors he carried in a case, he swiftly cut off Cardenio’s beard, dressed him in a gray jerkin of his own, and gave him a black cloak, leaving himself in his breeches and doublet. Cardenio looked so different from before that he wouldn’t have recognized himself in a mirror. Once this was done — and although the others had ridden on ahead while they were disguising themselves — they easily got out onto the high road before them, because the brambles and rough ground didn’t let the riders move as fast as those on foot. They then stationed themselves on the level ground at the mouth of the Sierra, and the moment Don Quixote and his companions emerged, the curate began studying him very deliberately, as if straining to recognize him. After staring at him a good while, he rushed toward him with open arms, exclaiming, “A happy meeting with the mirror of chivalry, my worthy countryman Don Quixote of La Mancha, the flower and cream of fine breeding, the protector and relief of the distressed, the quintessence of knights-errant!” And as he said it, he clasped the knee of Don Quixote’s left leg in his arms. Don Quixote, astonished by the stranger’s words and behavior, looked at him closely and finally recognized him. Amazed to see him there, he made strenuous efforts to dismount, but the curate wouldn’t allow it, at which Don Quixote said, “Permit me, señor licentiate — it isn’t fitting that I should be on horseback while so reverend a person as your worship goes on foot.”

“I won’t allow it under any circumstances,” said the curate. “Your mightiness must stay on horseback, because it is on horseback that you achieve the greatest deeds and adventures our age has ever seen. As for me, an unworthy priest, it will be quite enough to ride on the haunches of one of the mules belonging to these gentlefolk traveling with your worship, if they have no objection. And I’ll imagine I’m mounted on the steed Pegasus, or on the zebra or charger that carried the famous Moor, Muzaraque, who to this day lies enchanted in the great hill of Zulema, a short distance from the great Complutum.”

“I won’t consent even to that, señor licentiate,” Don Quixote answered. “And I know it will please my lady the princess, out of love for me, to order her squire to give up his mule’s saddle to your worship — he can sit behind, if the animal will carry them both.”

“It will, I’m certain,” said the princess, “and I’m just as certain that I won’t need to give my squire any orders. He is far too courteous and considerate to let a churchman travel on foot when he could ride.”

“So he is,” said the barber, and dismounting at once, he offered his saddle to the curate, who accepted it without needing much persuasion. But unluckily, as the barber was climbing up behind, the mule — a hired one, which is just another way of saying bad-tempered — lifted its hind hooves and let fly a couple of kicks in the air that would have made Master Nicholas wish his whole expedition in search of Don Quixote to the devil if they had caught him in the chest or the head. As it was, they startled him so badly that he tumbled to the ground, paying so little attention to his beard that it fell off, and when he found himself without it, all he could think to do was clap both hands over his face and groan that his teeth had been knocked out. When Don Quixote saw that whole bundle of beard lying detached, with no jaws and no blood, away from the face of the fallen squire, he exclaimed:
“By the living God, this is a great miracle! It has knocked the beard clean off his face and plucked it away, as neatly as if it had been shaved off on purpose.”

The curate, seeing the danger of his scheme being exposed, immediately snatched up the beard and hurried with it over to where Master Nicholas lay, still groaning. Pulling the barber’s head against his chest, he had the beard back on in an instant, murmuring some words over him that, he said, were a special charm for sticking on beards, as they would soon see. As soon as it was fixed, he stepped back, and the squire was as well-bearded and as whole as before. Don Quixote was astonished beyond measure, and he begged the curate to teach him that charm when there was a chance. He was convinced its power must extend beyond the sticking-on of beards — for clearly, where the beard had been torn away, the flesh must have been left mangled and lacerated, and anything that could heal all that had to be good for more than beards.

“And so it is,” said the curate, and he promised to teach it to him at the first opportunity. They then agreed that for the moment the curate should ride, and that the three of them would take turns on the mules until they reached the inn, which was perhaps six leagues from where they were.
So with three mounted — that is, Don Quixote, the princess, and the curate — and three on foot — Cardenio, the barber, and Sancho Panza — Don Quixote said to the damsel:
“Let your highness, my lady, lead the way, wherever pleases you best.” But before she could answer, the licentiate said:
“Toward which kingdom does your ladyship mean to direct our route? Toward Micomicon, perhaps? It must be — either that, or I know very little about kingdoms.”
She, primed on every point, understood that she was supposed to answer “Yes,” so she said, “Yes, señor, my road lies toward that very kingdom.”

“In that case,” said the curate, “we’ll have to pass straight through my village, and from there your worship will take the road to Cartagena, where, with luck, you’ll be able to board a ship. And if the wind is fair and the sea smooth and calm, in somewhat less than nine years you may come within sight of the great lake Meona — I mean Meotides — which lies little more than a hundred days’ journey this side of your highness’s kingdom.”

“Your worship is mistaken, señor,” she said, “because it isn’t even two years since I set out from there, and although I never once had good weather, here I am nonetheless, having come to see the one thing I longed for: my lord Don Quixote of La Mancha, whose fame reached my ears the moment I set foot in Spain and drove me to go in search of him, so I could commend myself to his courtesy and entrust the justice of my cause to the strength of his invincible arm.”

“Enough — no more praise,” Don Quixote broke in, “for I hate flattery of every kind, and even if this isn’t flattery, talk like that still offends my chaste ears. All I will say, señora, is that whatever strength my arm has or doesn’t have, every bit of what it may or may not have shall be devoted to your service until death. But leaving all that to its proper time, I would ask the señor licentiate to tell me what has brought him to these parts — alone, unattended, and so lightly dressed that it fills me with amazement.”

“I’ll answer that briefly,” the curate replied. “You should know, Señor Don Quixote, that Master Nicholas, our friend and barber, and I were on our way to Seville to collect some money that a relative of mine, who went off to the Indies many years ago, had sent me — and no small sum either, for it came to more than sixty thousand pieces of eight, full weight, which is no trifle. As we passed through this area yesterday, we were attacked by four highwaymen, who stripped us of everything, right down to our beards — and they took those off too, so completely that the barber found it necessary to put on a false one. Even this young man here” — and he pointed at Cardenio — “they transformed completely. But the best part is that the story going around the neighborhood says the men who attacked us belong to a band of galley slaves who, people say, were set free almost on this very spot by a man of such valor that, in defiance of the commissary and the guards, he released the whole lot of them. Beyond any doubt, the man must have been out of his mind, or else he is as great a scoundrel as they are — some man without heart or conscience, willing to turn the wolf loose among the sheep, the fox among the hens, the fly into the honey. He has cheated justice and defied his king and lawful master, since he defied his just commands. He has, I say, robbed the galleys of their feet, and stirred up the Holy Brotherhood, which has been quiet for many years; and in the end, he has done a deed that may cost him his soul without bringing his body any gain.” Sancho had told the curate and the barber about the adventure of the galley slaves, which his master had carried off with such glory, and so the curate, in bringing it up, laid it on thick to see what Don Quixote would say or do. The knight changed color at every word, not daring to admit that he himself had been the liberator of those fine people. “These, then,” said the curate, “were the men who robbed us — and may God in His mercy pardon the one who kept them from going to the punishment they deserved.”
